WarmResponse.title: WarmResponse

WarmSearchResponse.description: Result of a search-backend warm run: how long the priming query took.
WarmSearchResponse.title: WarmSearchResponse

WeightsChangeNote.description:
Tool-check verdicts the installed weights have outrun.

A re-pull changes the digest, and every verdict measured on the previous
weights stops counting - silently, because binding verdicts to weights is
what makes them trustworthy. Silence is right for the resolution and wrong
for a reader: a model's measured facts simply vanish, with an old failure
clamp evaporating alongside them. This is the notice that says so.

Derived, never stored. It is the probe log compared against the digest the
tag points at right now, so it appears the moment weights change and clears
itself the moment a check runs against the new ones - or the moment the tag
comes back to weights a check already covered. There is no dismissal to
record and nothing to clean up.

Null means the notice does not apply - which includes the ordinary "nothing
has ever been checked" case. That one is not a warning: it is what a fresh
model looks like, and the row already says it in plain words.

Attributes:
    depths: Every depth whose latest verdict was measured on other weights,
        weakest first ("fast" before "deep"). The last entry is the depth
        the two fields below describe - the fullest orphaned measurement of
        the set, on the same preference the measured facts use.
    earned: What that orphaned verdict earned, on the weights it actually
        measured. Reported so a reader can see what a re-check stands to
        recover; it is never a claim about the installed weights, and no
        part of the agency resolution reads it.
    measured_at: When that verdict was measured, always with an explicit
        UTC offset - it is rendered as a date beside other timestamps in
        this payload, and an offset-less stamp would be read as local time.
WeightsChangeNote.title: WeightsChangeNote

WorkspaceDefaultsOut.description:
The tenant's stored defaults plus the facts needed to render them.

Every stored field is nullable and null means UNSET - the tier below it in
the resolution chain decides. That is deliberately distinct from a value:
a null thinking default lets the per-turn heuristic run, where ``"auto"``
stored pins the heuristic explicitly.

Attributes:
    model: The workspace's default chat tag, or null.
    embedding_model: The tag retrieval embeds with, or null to let the
        deployment answer - which it does from the model its stored
        passages were written by, then from the one embedding model the
        server holds when it holds exactly one.
        Null therefore does NOT mean "no embedder": it means nobody has
        chosen one here.
    thinking: The workspace's default thinking mode, or null.
    web_search: The workspace's default web-search mode, or null.
    system_prompt: The persona every turn here opens with, or null when
        the deployment's own persona stands.
    context_ceiling: The largest window any turn may request, or null to
        leave the size to the deployment's configured default. It never
        exceeds the window the weights themselves admit; below that it is
        the deployment's affordance outright, so it can raise a window as
        readily as lower one.
    reranker: False when retrieval is forced dense-only; true or null when
        the deployment's reranker (if any) may run.
    reranker_status: What this deployment can actually do about that.
    min_context_ceiling: The smallest ceiling the API accepts.
    max_context_ceiling: The largest.
    max_system_prompt_chars: The longest persona the API accepts, so the
        page can say the limit rather than discover it in a 422.
WorkspaceDefaultsOut.title: WorkspaceDefaultsOut

WorkspaceDefaultsPatch.description:
The body of the workspace-defaults PATCH: the same per-field merge.

Every field this accepts is one some live read path already consults, and
that is the rule the page is held to - a stored default nothing reads is
a control that lies about having done something.

The model tag's SHAPE is checked here (length) and its grammar in the
service, through the same parser the management verbs use; its EXISTENCE
deliberately is not. An operator may set a default ahead of pulling the
weights, a remote server's inventory changes without this deployment
hearing about it, and the resolution chain already falls through a tag it
cannot honour - so refusing here would trade a working fall-through for a
validation failure against a listing that may be stale by the time the
turn runs.

Attributes:
    model: The workspace's default chat tag, or null to clear.
    embedding_model: The tag retrieval embeds with, or null to clear and
        let the deployment answer. Clearing is not the same as never
        having set it only in what it leaves behind: whichever tag wrote
        the stored passages goes on being observable, and the resolution
        falls back to it.
    thinking: The workspace's default thinking mode, or null to clear.
    web_search: The workspace's default web-search mode, or null to clear.
    system_prompt: The persona every turn opens with, or null to clear.
        A blank or whitespace-only value IS a clear, deliberately: the
        environment's ``SYSTEM_PROMPT=""`` kill switch has no workspace
        twin, so the emptied textarea means "fall back", never "silence
        the system prompt".
    context_ceiling: The largest window every turn is held to, or null to
        clear. Bounded at BOTH ends deliberately: never below the room a
        turn needs for its own answer, and never above a plausible window,
        because for a tag nothing declares this number is not a trim on
        somebody else's window - it is the one the turn requests.
    reranker: False to force dense-only retrieval, True to use the
        deployment's sidecar when it has one, null to clear.
WorkspaceDefaultsPatch.title: WorkspaceDefaultsPatch

post.description:
Store an uploaded file and queue it for parsing into the conversation.

The response is the attachment in its ``pending`` state; the client polls
:func:`get_attachment` until ``status`` reaches ``ready`` or ``failed``.
Returns 201: a new resource is created even though its content is not yet
retrievable.

delete.description:
Delete an uploaded file: its indexed text, its stored bytes, and its row.

Taking a file off a turn has to actually remove it. An upload is ingested
the moment it lands, so a file that was merely hidden from the composer
would still be retrievable, and the assistant would go on answering from a
document its owner believes is gone.

Deleting an already-deleted file is a 404, exactly as for an id that never
existed; a partial failure leaves the file addressable so the same request
can simply be retried.

get.description:
Return one attachment, for polling its ingestion status.

A malformed or foreign id is a 404, the same as an absent one: an id that
cannot address a resource, or addresses another tenant's, must not be
distinguishable from one that never existed.

Return one attachment's stored bytes as a download.

This is what makes a file the assistant produced actually reachable: the
``file`` stream event announces it and the reply's chip names it, and both
are decoration until the bytes can be fetched.

The whole object is read and answered in one response rather than streamed.
That is a deliberate bound, not an oversight: uploads are capped by
``attachment_max_bytes`` and generated files far lower, so the ceiling is
known and small, and a streaming variant would need a new seam method on
every storage backend to earn nothing at these sizes.

Which files are served is :func:`_refuse_unless_servable`'s decision - a
``ready`` file, and a person's own upload whose INGESTION failed - and every
refusal carries its own reason. A row that claims to hold bytes that are not
there answers 404 rather than 500: the client asked an answerable question
and deserves an answer, while the inconsistency is the server's to log.

A malformed or foreign id is a 404, exactly as for the metadata route: an id
that addresses another user's file must not be distinguishable from one that
never existed.

head.description:
Answer whether the file can be downloaded, without moving its bytes.

The same question :func:`download_attachment` answers, reaching the same
codes (200, 409, 410, 404, 503) without reading the object - the row and one
``exists`` call on the storage seam are the whole cost.

That is what earns it a place. A client that CHECKS before downloading -
so a file that aged out explains itself instead of saving to disk as an
error document - would otherwise spend two whole-object reads per saved
file, and the download route is rate-limited into a small budget precisely
because it buffers one. With this, checking is ordinary traffic and only the
file itself is expensive.

Nothing is being replaced here: FastAPI overwrites the HEAD that Starlette
adds beside a GET (``fastapi.routing`` assigns the declared methods
verbatim), so without this route the method is a plain 405.

``Content-Length`` is the row's recorded size, which is the length of the
object as it was written. It is second-hand by construction - the GET, which
reads the blob, remains the authority - but quoting it is closer to RFC 9110
("send the same header fields a GET would") than the ``0`` a bodiless
response would otherwise advertise, which is a plain lie about the file.

200.description: The file is there, and these headers describe it.

get.description:
Finish a sign-in: verify what came back, mint a session, and land.

Unauthenticated by necessity - the provider's redirect arrives here with no
session - which makes it the most exposed route in this router. Every check
the flow depends on happens before anything is written: the ``state`` must
match this browser's own cookie and is then consumed atomically, the code is
exchanged with the PKCE verifier, and the id_token's signature, issuer,
audience, expiry and nonce are all verified before an identity is admitted
or a row is touched.

``error`` is the provider's own refusal (the person pressed Cancel, most
often). It is reported as a refusal rather than as a fault: nothing is
broken and there is nothing to retry differently.

Start a sign-in: redirect the browser to the identity provider.

The pending attempt (its nonce, its PKCE verifier, and where to land) is
stashed under a single-use ``state`` for ten minutes; the callback consumes
it or it expires. The same ``state`` goes to the browser as a short-lived
cookie, which is what ties the eventual callback to THIS browser - see
:data:`LOGIN_STATE_COOKIE_NAME`.

``next`` must be a RELATIVE path. An absolute or scheme-bearing value is
discarded rather than followed - a sign-in endpoint that will redirect
anywhere is an open redirector wearing the most trustworthy hat on the site.

Answers 404 where no issuer is configured: there is no sign-in on that
deployment, so the route genuinely names nothing rather than being a thing
that exists and refuses.

parameters.description: Relative path to land on afterwards.
parameters.name: next

schema.description: Relative path to land on afterwards.
schema.title: Next

post.description:
End the current session, if there is one.

Deletes the server-side record, so the cookie is worthless the moment this
returns even if a copy of it survives somewhere - which is the whole reason
sessions are server-side rather than a signed token.

Answers 204 whether or not a session was found, and whether or not login is
configured. Signing out is idempotent by nature, and a sign-out that reports
"there was nothing to sign out of" tells a caller about somebody else's
session state for the price of a guessed cookie.

get.description:
Report who the caller is, and whether this deployment has login at all.

The frontend's first call. It resolves the principal through the SAME path
every other route does, so what it reports is what a real request would act
as - not a second, parallel reading of the cookie that could disagree with
the first.

401 ``auth_required`` where login is on and there is no valid session, which
is the response the client turns into a hop to the sign-in page.

post.description:
Stream a chat completion as SSE (meta, token, thinking, status, citation, error, done).

The stream slot is claimed (or a 429 raised) by :func:`hold_stream_slot`
before any work and released when the request unwinds, on every outcome.
Conversation resolution is awaited before the response starts, so lookup
(400/404) failures reach clients as problem+json instead of a broken event
stream. Failures after streaming begins stay in-band SSE error events -
except retrieval failures, which degrade to an ungrounded answer.

get.description:
Return one page of the tenant's conversations, pinned first then newest activity.

Pinned threads lead the page so a pin survives paging: a client that reads
only the first page still sees every pinned thread, however much newer
activity sits behind it.

post.description:
Create an empty conversation and return its summary.

A conversation normally comes into being with its first chat turn. This
mints one up front so a client can attach a file before that turn exists -
an upload must name the conversation it belongs to, and there is nothing to
name until the first message otherwise. The new conversation has no title
yet; the first message derives one, exactly as an implicitly created
conversation does.

delete.description:
Delete a conversation, its messages, its ephemeral vectors and its files.

Everything downstream of the row is best-effort privacy hygiene with a
sweep behind it, because the conversation delete has already committed and
must not be reported as failed once it has:

- Session-scoped vectors belong to the conversation, so they go with it
  rather than waiting for the TTL sweep. A store failure only logs, and the
  TTL sweep is genuinely the backstop - for the web pages and other ephemeral
  chunks that carry one.
- Uploaded files outlive the row on purpose (the FK is ON DELETE SET NULL),
  leaving a row that still knows where the bytes are. The attachment ids are
  read BEFORE the delete - afterwards nothing links them to this
  conversation - and handed to a job that removes the file's indexed text,
  its bytes and its row. If the queue is down, the rows now have no
  conversation, which is exactly what the periodic attachment sweep collects.

  A file's chunks are session-scoped, so the drop above normally takes them
  too - but only normally, and that is why the job removes them again. The
  drop is best-effort (it may have just failed), and an ingest still in flight
  can write its chunks in behind it. Nothing else would catch either case:
  attachment chunks carry NO TTL (they have to outlive the session, or an
  uploaded file would stop grounding two hours after it arrived), so the TTL
  sweep is not a backstop for them, and once the row is gone nothing left in
  the system can even name them.

get.description:
Return one conversation with its messages in chronological order, plus its files.

The top-level attachments list exists to restore the COMPOSER. A client puts
back the files no message carries: those were uploaded and ingested but never
sent, so a reopened conversation shows them again rather than losing a draft
the server is still holding.

That is why files the assistant GENERATED are excluded from it. A generated
file is never the user's unsent draft - nobody chose it, and the client tells
a draft from a sent file only by "no message carries it", which a generated
file can satisfy honestly (its turn saved no reply, or is still paused at a
confirmation). Left in, the assistant's own document would appear as a chip
in the composer and ride out attached to the user's next question.

The exclusion is deliberately HERE and not in the repository: the delete path
below reads the same list to collect blobs to reclaim, and it must see every
row. Generated files are still reported per MESSAGE, on the reply that made
them (``meta["attachments"]``), which is what a transcript renders them from.

patch.description:
Apply the provided fields; ``settings`` merges per field, never wholesale.

An update that changes nothing - an empty body, a title already at its
requested value, a settings patch the stored values already satisfy - does
not bump ``updated_at``, so a spurious PATCH cannot reorder the sidebar.
(Re-submitting the same title does still commit when it is the first time
the name is recorded as a human choice; see below.) A real settings change commits but
does not bump ``updated_at`` either: settings are metadata, not
activity, and flipping a composer control must not resurface an old
thread. Only a title change counts as activity.

A title written here is stamped as MANUAL, which is what stops the
background namer - now or after a later edit of the opening question -
from replacing a name its owner chose.

``pinned`` is intent, not a time: the server stamps ``pinned_at`` itself, so
a client clock can never decide where a row sits in the pinned group.
Pinning is metadata like settings, so it commits without bumping
``updated_at`` - a pin must not resurface an old thread in the recent list
it just left.

The row is read FOR UPDATE because the settings merge is a
read-merge-write: without the lock, two overlapping single-field saves
could both read the same base and the later commit would silently drop
the earlier one's axis.

get.description:
Estimate the window's fill for this conversation before any turn runs.

The eager reading behind the composer's context meter: on pane load or a
model switch, the client asks what the next prompt already opens with
instead of waiting for a turn to report it. ``model`` is the composer's
pin, honoured verbatim; absent, the default resolves through the same
stored chain a turn would use. Character arithmetic over stored rows -
no generation, no model load.

The browser's return leg: consume the state, exchange, and go home.

Always answers a 302 to the Integrations page with NO query string - the
authorization code must not ride into another access log, and the page
reads connection status from the API rather than the URL. A denial or a
failed exchange still consumes the state (single use), logs the reason,
and redirects; the card simply stays disconnected.

The literal redirect URI every consent this deployment starts will use.

Providers only deliver the authorization code to a URL registered on the
app, so the operator must paste this exact value into the provider's app
settings BEFORE connecting. Deployment config (`OAUTH_REDIRECT_BASE_URL`
plus the callback path), never a secret - any member may read it.

The curated presets: prefill values plus setup notes, display-ordered.

Static, read-only metadata - no credential, no tenant data - so any member
may read it; connecting anything still goes through the admin-gated
routes above.

List the tenant's registered servers (enabled and disabled), name-ordered.

Carries whether this deployment can seal credentials at all, so a client can
say so BEFORE an admin types one - see the schema's note.

post.description: Register a new MCP server. Admin-gated; a duplicate name is a 409.

Probe a server (initialize + tools/list ONLY) and report its tools or an error.

Always 200: a target being down is a diagnostic result carried in
``error.code``, not a fault of this API. Never runs a tool. Admin-gated: a
handshake reaches an arbitrary URL, so it is as SSRF-adjacent as registration.

delete.description:
Delete a server, its shared workspace credential, and any OAuth grant.

A row the deployment's environment currently seeds is REFUSED with a 409
instead, because deleting it would not last: the bootstrap is get-or-create
by name, so the row returns at the next restart with its credential and its
tool toggles gone. A button that appears to work and quietly undoes itself
is worse than one that explains the constraint, and the durable off switch
already exists - ``enabled`` survives every restart precisely because
seeding never overwrites an existing row. This is the config-owned carve-out
of the disclose-and-migrate rule: nothing here can repair the request, since
what recreates the row lives in the deployment's environment, not in the
request. The refusal comes FIRST, before any destructive step - a delete
that is going to be refused must not revoke an OAuth grant on its way out.

The row and its workspace secrets go in one transaction. An OAuth-connected
server is REVOKED upstream first (best effort) and both of its sealed
secrets - the token bundle and the client registration - are deleted with
it: they are separate rows with no foreign key to ``mcp_servers``, keyed on
a name derivable only from the id and URL that are about to vanish, so
leaving them would strand a live third-party refresh token that no API or
UI could ever list, let alone revoke. A dead provider or a missing
``SECRET_MASTER_KEY`` is logged and does not block the delete - an
undeletable row would be the worse failure.

User credentials across members are left as harmless orphans, and here they
genuinely are: every credential is keyed on the server's stable id (see
:func:`credential_secret_name`), so a later server - even one recreated under
the same name - gets a fresh id and can never derive the orphaned name, and
the SecretStore reaches only the acting principal's rows regardless.

get.description: Return one registered server's metadata (never its credential).

patch.description:
Patch a server (enable/disable, re-point, rescope, edit config).

An empty body is a no-op. Any real change invalidates the cached source so the
next turn rebuilds from the committed row.

delete.description: Clear a server's credential (scope-dependent gate, like the write).

get.description: Return whether a server has a credential, plus its metadata hint - no plaintext.

put.description:
Seal a server's credential (write-only). Returns metadata + last4, never plaintext.

Scope follows the server: a workspace server's shared credential (admin only)
or the acting member's own for a user-scoped server. 503 when
``SECRET_MASTER_KEY`` is unset - never plaintext, never a throwaway key.

post.description:
Start a workspace OAuth consent; answer with the provider URL to open.

Admin-gated like every registry write. With ``endpoints`` supplied the
request is the generic-provider path (no discovery, no resource binding);
without, the authorization server is discovered from the MCP server
itself. Nothing here runs a tool or stores a token - the callback does the
storing, and abandoning the returned URL leaves only an expiring row.
Revoke the server's grant (best effort) and delete the sealed bundle.

Re-test a registered server using its STORED credential (or a one-shot override).

Unlike the pre-save ``POST /servers/test-connection`` (an ad-hoc URL + typed
key), this probes a saved row with the credential the chat path would send, so a
connected-and-healthy server no longer reports ``auth_rejected`` on a
credential-less probe. An ``oauth`` row resolves its grant's live bearer through
the SAME helper the chat path uses (renewing a stale token in place), so a
connected server tests exactly as it would list. Scope-gated like the credential
ops (a workspace server's shared credential is admin-only; a user-scoped server
tests the acting member's own). Always 200 - a down target is a diagnostic in
``error.code``, never a credential value. The handshake never runs a tool.

delete.description:
Remove one source's passages from the knowledge base.

Nothing in a knowledge base is undeletable - it is a corpus somebody
curates - so this refuses nothing, and answers with the count instead of a
bare 204. An id that matches nothing is a successful zero rather than a 404:
there is no row whose absence could be checked, and "already gone" is an
honest answer to "remove this". The count is what tells the two apart.

Copies in every vector space go, not only the one the active embedder
reads, so a source stranded by an embedding-model change is genuinely
removable rather than merely invisible.

get.description:
List the workspace's stored knowledge, newest ingest first.

Every source is reported, including any left in a vector space an earlier
embedding model wrote: those are still stored and still occupy room, and
hiding them would leave an operator unable to see - let alone remove - the
thing a model change stranded. Each row says whether the ACTIVE embedder can
reach it, which is the only sense in which a stored document is currently
part of what answers are grounded on.

A workspace that has never ingested anything answers with an empty list
rather than a 404: an empty knowledge base is a state, not a missing
resource.

The embedder is not required here, and that is deliberate - a deployment
whose embedder configuration is broken is exactly when someone needs to see
what is stored. Every row then reads unreachable, which is true.

post.description:
Read one uploaded file and store its text in the knowledge base.

Returns 200, not 201: ingestion is idempotent per document id, so uploading
the same file twice updates what is stored rather than creating a second
copy of it, and callers are meant to re-run freely after an interruption.

Synchronous by design - the response arrives when the text is genuinely
searchable. See :mod:`app.services.knowledge` for why there is no background
job: without a table there is nowhere to record a status a client could
poll, and every failure this file can produce is answered right here
instead.

The bytes are parsed and discarded. Nothing stores the original file, so
what lands in the knowledge base is its text and nothing else.

get.description:
List the workspace's members, oldest first.

Each row carries whether the deployment's configuration floors it to admin,
so the console can render that account's role as fixed and say why rather
than offering a control whose effect the next sign-in would undo.

patch.description:
Set one member's role to ``admin`` or ``member``.

Refused with a 409 when the change would leave the workspace without an
administrator, or when the account's role is set by the deployment's own
configuration - both messages name what to do instead. An admin may demote
themselves as long as somebody else can still administer the workspace.

No delete or deactivate verb here: an account that must lose access loses it
at the identity provider, which is the only place that decision holds.

get.description:
Return the models this server holds, and what is known about each.

The ``models`` key is the provider's live list (the UI selector depends on
its shape); ``entries`` describes each held tag - the role the runtime's
report derives for it, and the capabilities that report plus the stored
declarations resolve. The chat ones are what a conversation can be pinned
to, so a ``role`` repeats across the list: filter on it, never key on it.

Every row is a model the server actually holds. A menu that also listed
models nobody had downloaded was a menu of things a picker could only
refuse, and against a remote host it described a machine that does not
exist - so the inventory is the list.

``server`` describes where the model server is and whether it is reached
with credentials, read from configuration alone so it is as true under a
stub provider as a live one. It is what lets a client warn that a model
server outside this deployment is unprotected - the server authenticates
nothing itself.

The ``thinking`` capability on every row resolves through the SAME chain a
turn does, stored declarations and unconfirmed measurements included. This
list feeds the composer, and the composer sits beside a management card
that resolves the full chain - two answers about one model on two screens
is exactly the disagreement worth paying for.

What it costs, stated plainly because it is not free: each row pays one
capability probe (concurrent, bounded, and cached for minutes) plus, on a
cold cache, one declaration read and up to four probe-log reads. The rows
are resolved CONCURRENTLY behind the same caches the chat path fills, and
the first read that cannot reach the store stops the rest - so a database
that is down costs this endpoint one timeout, not one per row.

post.description:
Declare how much this model may be allowed to drive.

The console's writer for the ceiling axis. A declaration is a CEILING and
only a ceiling: raising it withdraws the human objection and nothing more,
because ``min(CEILING, EARNED)`` still holds the model at whatever a
digest-bound deep check has proven on the server being served from. So an
``agentic`` declaration on an unproven model is STORED and takes effect the
moment a deep check passes - which is why the response reports ``earned``
and ``effective`` beside the value written, rather than echoing the write
and letting a page claim a change that did not happen.

A DOWN-clamp is the opposite: ``min()`` needs no evidence to lower
something, so it applies to the next turn.

Admin-gated with the other verbs that act. Errors map to problem+json: 403
(not an admin), 422 (the name is not a usable model name, the mode is not
one this build knows, or the runtime exposes no weights digest to bind a
claim about weights to), 404 (the backend does not hold these weights), 503
(the model server is unreachable).

Make this model the workspace default every unpinned conversation follows.

The console's counterpart to the successor a delete already writes, and it
validates the same way: the tag has to be installed and has to serve a role
that can drive a chat turn. A default nothing can route to is the worst
kind of stored setting - it is accepted silently and surfaces one turn
later, on somebody else's question, as a substitution note.

Admin-gated with the other verbs that act. Errors map to problem+json: 403
(not an admin), 422 (the name is not a usable model name), 404 (the backend
does not hold these weights), 409 (the tag serves a locked role), 503 (the
model server is unreachable).

Measure an embedder's relevance bands and judge the retrieval floors.

The retrieval-side sibling of the tool check, and a plain JSON answer
rather than a stream: it embeds a fixed corpus of query/answer/distractor
triplets, both with and without the query prefix under test, and reports
the two score bands that came out. Seconds, not minutes - which is why
there is nothing to stream.

The answer either VALIDATES the floors already declared for this embedder
or PROPOSES a pair derived from the measured bands, with the derivation
spelled out. Nothing is applied: ``RAG_MIN_SCORE`` and ``RAG_REL_MARGIN``
decide what every answer in the deployment may cite, so a number that
changes them is a person's decision, not a probe's.

Errors map to problem+json: 403 (not an admin), 422 (unusable name), 400
(the tag is a declared non-embedding model, or no embedder is configured
and none was named), 404 (the backend does not hold those weights), 409 (a
check or a tool check is already running), 503 (the model server is
unreachable, or it answered with vectors no score could be matched to).

get.description:
Return the management view: the inventory joined to measured and declared state.

Read-only. Every row carries what the runtime REPORTS about the weights, what
provider currently holds the weights, what a tool-check actually MEASURED
on them, and which management verbs apply - assembled per request, with
nothing stored and nothing predicted. Each row also says what is still set
to use that model: the deployment's own chat pair withdraws Delete (the
one refusal a request cannot resolve), while a pin count and the
workspace-default flag ride along so the confirm dialog can disclose what
a delete will move - pins cleared, the default handed to a successor
named in the same request. The payload carries
whether the vectors already stored are still reachable by the configured
embedding model too, which is the one fact about the locked embedding role
that the lock itself cannot guarantee.

A provider that cannot be reached is a 503 rather than a page with
every row marked "not installed": those flags are the point of the view,
and inverting them all would invite re-pulling models that are already
here. An unreachable VECTOR store is not a 503, though - it makes the
stranded report say "unknown" and leaves the rest of the page useful, and
it is bounded by its own short timeout so a black-holed store cannot hold
the page either. The AppError handler renders the problem+json body.

ADMIN-ONLY, and now genuinely so. The response carries a DEPLOYMENT-WIDE
space inventory - every collection, its point count, and which embedding
models wrote it, summed across every tenant - which is operator information
rather than anything a member's own work needs. The gate was declared but
unenforceable while every caller was the single seeded user; a configured
login makes the role real, so it is wired here alongside the three verbs
that ACT (pull, delete, and the preflight before a pull).

post.description:
Ask the registry whether a name exists and what it would cost to download.

On demand only - nothing about rendering a list calls this. Admin-gated with
the verb it precedes: it is the endpoint that makes the backend issue an
outbound request, and it would be odd for a caller to be able to shop the
registry but not to download. A malformed or unsafe name is a 422 before any
request leaves the process, and a backend that cannot download models at all
is a 400 rather than an answer about a tag it could never fetch; every other
outcome, including an unreachable registry, is a 200 whose ``status`` says
honestly how much is known.

Download a model, streaming its progress as SSE (progress, done, error).

Everything a download can be refused for is decided before any work, so a
refusal arrives as problem+json rather than as an event on a stream a
progress bar is already attached to: a malformed name (422), a backend with
no download verb (400), and a second download of a tag already being
fetched (409). Failures after that are in-band ``error`` events, because by
then the connection IS a progress stream.

A successful download continues into the fast tool check unless the body
turns it off, on the same stream - see :mod:`app.schemas.models` for how
the ``done`` frame keeps the two outcomes separate.

get.description:
Return what the serving runtime is holding in memory right now.

The live counterpart to the management view's declared and measured facts:
that one says what a model IS, this one says what is loaded this second.
Read straight off the seam's residency view - the same one the verify job
asserts GPU residency with - and reported exactly as the runtime gave it,
including a model nothing here describes.

A runtime that does not report residency answers ``reported: false`` with an
empty list rather than an error: not knowing is a normal state for a backend
that loads one model at process start, and it is emphatically not the same
answer as "nothing is loaded". An unreachable runtime lands there too, since
the seam's residency hooks are best-effort by design and a page that fails
over one small widget would be a worse page.

ADMIN-ONLY, gated with the management view above and for the same reason:
what the shared model server is holding right now is operator information
about the deployment, not about the caller's own work.

post.description:
Store what a tool check measured about this model's think flag.

The confirmation step of the think check: a check watches how the weights
treat the flag, and this is where an operator agrees that the measurement
is how the deployment should route the model from now on. The stored value
is the MEASURED one - the body names a model and nothing else, so a caller
cannot declare a mode nothing observed.

Admin-gated with the other verbs that act. Errors map to problem+json: 403
(not an admin), 422 (the name is not a usable model name, or no check has
measured the installed weights - confirming without evidence is refused),
404 (the backend does not hold these weights), 503 (the model server is
unreachable).

Pair a direct-answer model with the partner that serves its thinking turns.

A PREFERENCE axis: it says how this deployment wants two tags used, not
what either checkpoint is, so it follows the tags across a re-pull rather
than retiring with the weights.

The partner is refused unless its think mode already RESOLVES to ``always``
or ``hybrid`` - through the one chain a turn and the management card both
read, never through a declaration invented here. Pairing two direct-answer
models would produce a thinking toggle that quietly changed nothing, and an
unmeasured partner is that same offer made on no evidence.

Admin-gated with the other verbs that act. Errors map to problem+json: 403
(not an admin), 422 (either name is unusable, the pair names one tag twice,
or nothing establishes that the partner can reason), 404 (the backend does
not hold one of the two), 503 (the model server is unreachable).

Declare whether this model may reason and call tools in the same turn.

The console's writer for the capability axis, gated exactly as the ceiling's
``agentic`` rung is and by the same mechanism - the fold, never a refusal
here. A GRANT is stored whatever the log holds and reaches a turn only once
a deep check has passed the reasoning-with-tools case on these weights, at
the running harness version and on the host being served from; a re-pull, a
harness edit or a move to another model server retires it through that same
fold. So the response reports ``effective`` beside what was written, rather
than echoing the write and letting a page claim a capability the model was
not given.

A REVOCATION is the opposite and applies to the next turn: the failure this
axis guards is silent - reasoning plus tools on an incapable pair returns an
EMPTY answer, not an error - so turning it off must never wait for evidence.

Admin-gated with the other verbs that act. Errors map to problem+json: 403
(not an admin), 422 (the name is not a usable model name, or the runtime
exposes no weights digest to bind a claim about weights to), 404 (the
backend does not hold these weights), 503 (the model server is
unreachable).

Measure a model's tool-calling, streaming each finished sample as SSE.

Streamed rather than answered, because a deep check runs twenty-six
exchanges over several minutes and a silent POST for that long is
indistinguishable from a hang. Refusals are decided before the response
begins and arrive as problem+json: 422 (unusable name), 404 (the backend
does not hold those weights), 409 (a probe is already running), 403 (not an
admin), 503 (the model server is unreachable). Everything after that is an
in-band ``verify_error`` frame.

The run evicts the chat model and the embedder to measure a fresh load, and
re-warms both afterwards whatever its outcome - see
:mod:`app.services.model_verify` for the full order and why it is that one.

Load a chat model and prime its prompt cache with the system prompt.

Runs a one-token generation through the real chat prompt so the FIRST
real turn does not pay the model load plus the system-prompt evaluation
(tens of seconds on small, partially-offloaded GPUs). With no ``model``
in the body, the warmed default resolves through the same stored chain a
chat turn uses - workspace default, then env override, then profile
binding - including the missing-model substitution, so what gets primed
is what a default turn would actually run (a remote server rarely holds
the local profile's tags).

"The real chat prompt" includes the TOOL BLOCK a tools-offered turn opens
with. A chat template renders the offered tool list into its system region,
so on a deployment with tools registered the block is most of the standing
prefix - and a prompt cache is prefix-matched, so a warm that omitted it
primed a head no real turn ever sends. The same collaborators a chat turn
is handed are therefore resolved here, and the reported ``prompt_tokens``
is the size of the prefix that was actually primed.

"The same stored chain" now covers the THINKING default as well, and not
as a refinement: a workspace that reasons by default routes its turns to a
different tag on a paired profile, so warming the pair's default member
would prime weights no turn runs, and the first question would evict them
to load the ones it needs. The window ceiling rides along for the
mechanically similar reason - a differently sized request restarts the
runner. Blocks until the warm generation finishes; `make warm` is the
intended caller.

A ``model`` that IS named does not have to be the exact tag. It is
resolved against what the server holds: an exact tag wins (the
``:latest`` and publisher-namespace spellings are equivalent, and case is
not identity), otherwise a fragment matching exactly one installed tag
resolves to it, and the response names whichever model was warmed. A
fragment matching several is refused with the candidates rather than
guessed through, and one reached by fragment is also refused when it
cannot serve a chat turn - an exact tag is honoured either way, since only
the inferred half can be wrong about which model was meant. A server whose
inventory cannot be read resolves nothing and takes the name as given.

Errors map to problem+json: 404 (model not pulled, no installed model
matches the name, or nothing on the server can chat), 400 (the name
matched several installed models or resolved to one that cannot chat -
both decided before the model server is called - or the model server
rejected the request), 503 (model server unreachable).

Load this workspace's embedding model into the model server.

Primes the embedding model so the first ingest or retrieval of a session
does not pay a multi-second cold load (the stall a first `/rag/ingest`
otherwise shows). Which model that is is not a caller's choice - it defines
the vector space - so ``model`` in the body is ignored here and the same
resolution a retrieval runs through decides; ``keep_alive`` is honored.
Errors map to problem+json: 404 (nothing resolves an embedding model), 503
(model not pulled or the model server is unreachable). ``prompt_tokens`` is
always null - an embedder has no prompt-prefix cache to report.

Prime the web-search backend so the first real search of a session is fast.

Issues one throwaway query to SearXNG so the DNS cache, connection pool, and
lazy-loaded workers are warm before a user's first web-search turn - the
turn that otherwise times out on a cold fan-out ("first search fails, second
works"). Errors map to problem+json: 404 when web search is not configured
(``SEARCH_PROVIDER=none``, or ``SEARXNG_URL`` unset), 503 when the search
backend is unreachable. Called by `make warm`; also fired in the background
at startup.

delete.description:
Remove a downloaded model, moving the stored state that named it.

Conversation pins on the tag are cleared in the same transaction (those
threads follow the workspace default), and deleting the workspace default
itself requires ``replacement`` - the validated successor written before
the weights go. The response says what changed; every refusal explains
itself.

Errors map to problem+json: 403 (not an admin), 422 (the name or the
replacement is not a usable model name), 400 (the backend cannot remove
models at all), 404 (it does not hold this one), 409 (the role is locked,
an embedding model is still active or referenced by stored passages, the
tag is the deployment's own chat pair, or it is the workspace default
without a usable successor), 503 (the model server is unreachable).

post.description:
Ingest structured records: chunk, embed, and store them for retrieval.

Synchronous by design for structured records (file uploads get a
background pipeline in a later phase): a maximum-size request (100 items
of 50k characters) embeds a few thousand chunks and can take minutes on
a CPU-pinned embedder. Ingestion is idempotent per document id, so a
timed-out or aborted call heals by simply re-running it.

Returns 200 (not 201) because re-ingesting existing documents is an
update, not a creation, and callers are encouraged to re-run freely.

A ``session_id`` must name one of the caller's own conversations (404
otherwise) - see :func:`_require_own_session`. Without that, an id lifted
from a URL would let anything be planted in another user's session scope,
where their next turn retrieves and cites it as their own stored material.

Similarity-search stored chunks (best hits first).

Searches the tenant's whole knowledge base unless ``collection`` narrows
it to one named corpus; ``session_id`` additionally searches that
session's ephemeral chunks. Scores are cosine similarities from the dense
search (or reranker relevance where a reranker is wired).

A ``session_id`` must name one of the caller's own conversations (404
otherwise) - see :func:`_require_own_session`. That scope holds uploaded
file text, fetched pages and records fetched under a per-user credential,
so reading it is a permission question, not a validation one.

get.description:
Return the workspace's stored defaults and what this deployment can honour.

Every value may be null, which means UNSET: the next tier of the
resolution chain decides that axis. The reranker status says whether a
sidecar exists for the toggle to govern at all, and the ceiling bounds and
the system-prompt length limit are what a write will accept - all facts
about the deployment, so a page never has to infer them from a failed save.

patch.description:
Change some of the workspace defaults, leaving the rest exactly as they were.

A per-field merge, never a whole-blob write: a field absent from the body
is untouched, an explicit ``null`` clears it, and a value overwrites. That
is what lets two controls save at once without either dropping the
other's field - and the read-merge-write holds a row lock so the two
genuinely serialize. Unknown keys are refused (422) rather than stored
where nothing would ever read them.

Committed before responding, so the page's next read - and the very next
chat turn - see what was just saved. The response is built from the merge's
own result rather than by re-reading the row: they are the same answer, and
a second read is a query whose only job is to agree with the first.

get.description: Liveness probe.

Readiness probe: report every backing service, and 503 if a required one is down.

Answers 200 when the database, the job queue and the vector store are all
reachable, and 503 otherwise. The model server, the search sidecar and the
reranker are reported for visibility but never change the status code:
the model server is routinely remote and slow to load, and the other two
are optional by design, so a failure there degrades the app rather than
disabling it.
